concept.title: Reducing Interference
concept.shortdesc: Wireless interference can reduce Wi-Fi speed, signal quality, and connection stability. Identify and reduce sources of interference to improve Wi-Fi performance.

section.title: Overview
section.p: Wireless interference occurs when another signal or a physical obstruction affects communication between the and client devices.
Interference can reduce data transfer rates, delay network communication, weaken the Wi-Fi signal, or disconnect client devices.
section.note: Start with simple changes. Move the router and client devices away from appliances, metal objects, and other wireless equipment.
Measure signal strength, noise, channel utilization, and packet retransmissions before you change the wireless configuration.

section.title: Types of Interference
section.p: Wireless signals and physical obstructions can affect Wi-Fi performance.

dlentry.dd: Wireless interference occurs when another device sends signals on the same or a nearby frequency.
Physical interference occurs when walls, floors, furniture, or other objects weaken or reflect the Wi-Fi signal.
Co-channel interference occurs when nearby Wi-Fi networks use the same channel. Devices on the channel must share the available transmission time.
Adjacent-channel interference occurs when nearby Wi-Fi networks use overlapping channels.

section.title: Sources of Wireless Interference
section.p: The following equipment can cause wireless interference:

ul.li: Nearby Wi-Fi routers and access points
Poorly shielded USB 3.0 devices and cables

section.note: A nearby device does not always cause interference. The effect depends on the operating frequency, distance, signal strength, and network environment.

section.title: Physical Obstructions
section.p: Physical objects can absorb, weaken, or reflect Wi-Fi signals. Signal loss can increase when the signal passes through multiple obstructions.
The following objects and materials can affect the Wi-Fi signal:

ul.li: Aquariums and other large containers of water

section.p: Reduce the number of obstructions between the and wireless client devices.
For more information, see .

section.title: Methods to Reduce Interference
section.p: Use the following methods to reduce interference:

ul.li: Put the in a central, open, and elevated location.
Increase the distance between the router and potential sources of interference.
Keep the router away from metal objects and enclosed spaces.
Reduce the number of physical obstructions between the router and client devices.
Test the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands on compatible devices.
Keep automatic channel selection enabled unless the network has a persistent connection problem.
Use Ethernet for stationary devices that require a stable connection.
Disconnect wireless devices that are not in use.
Keep the firmware on the up to date.
Use the or when physical obstructions prevent sufficient coverage.

section.note: Make one change at a time. Test the network after each change. This method helps you identify the change that improves network performance.

section.title: Wi-Fi Band Selection
section.p: The 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands can experience different levels of interference. Test both bands and use the band that provides a stable connection in the required location.
section.note: If a nearby device causes interference on the 2.4 GHz band, connect a compatible client device to the 5 GHz band and test the connection again.
section.p: For more information, see .

section.title: Wireless Channel Selection
section.p: A Wi-Fi band contains multiple wireless channels. Nearby networks that use the same or overlapping channels can reduce Wi-Fi performance.
Keep automatic channel selection enabled when wireless conditions change frequently.
section.note: Do not change the wireless channel unless automatic channel selection does not provide a stable connection.
Use a wireless analysis tool to examine nearby networks and channel utilization. Select a permitted channel with low utilization if manual channel selection is necessary.
The default 5 GHz configuration in this guide uses . Evaluate the wireless environment and applicable regional requirements before you use this value.

section.title: Channel Width
section.p: Channel width determines the amount of wireless spectrum that a Wi-Fi connection uses.
A wide channel can support higher data rates when the wireless environment is clear. However, it can experience more interference in a congested environment.
The default 5 GHz configuration in this guide uses . Use a narrower channel width if the network experiences persistent interference or high channel utilization.
section.note: Do not select the widest channel only to increase the maximum data rate. Select a channel width that provides a stable connection in the actual network environment.

section.title: Multiple Access Points and Mesh Nodes
section.p: Multiple access points or mesh nodes can improve Wi-Fi coverage. Incorrect placement or channel selection can also increase interference.
Put each or where it has a reliable connection to the network and can provide coverage to the required area.
Configure nearby access points to use different, non-overlapping channels when manual channel planning is necessary.
Use a wired backhaul connection when possible. A wired backhaul reduces the wireless capacity used for communication between network devices.

section.title: USB Device Interference
section.p: A USB 3.0 device or cable near the can affect 2.4 GHz wireless communication.
Increase the distance between the USB device, its cable, and the wireless antennas. Use a correctly shielded USB cable.
section.note: This information applies only when a device is connected to the .

section.title: Evaluate the Network
section.p: Test the Wi-Fi connection in the locations where users frequently connect wireless devices.
Test the connection when a potential source of interference is active. Test the connection again when the source is inactive. Compare the results.
section.note: If the connection becomes slow or unstable near an appliance, increase the distance between the appliance and the router or client device.
Record the test location, band, channel, channel width, signal strength, channel utilization, throughput, latency, and packet loss. Use the same test conditions when you compare results.

section.title: Persistent Interference
section.p: If interference continues after you move the router and test both Wi-Fi bands, review the wireless channel settings.
If physical obstructions prevent sufficient coverage, use the or to extend Wi-Fi coverage.
If the connection remains slow, weak, or unstable, refer to the applicable topic reference.
